title: Pepper — 3yo guinea pig: straining to urinate with blood in the bedding
presentation: 3-year-old female guinea pig, hunched and vocalising when passing urine for four days. The owner has found pink staining on the bedding and she is eating less hay than usual.

stages.title: Separate urinary from reproductive bleeding
stages.briefing: Weight 890 g, down 60 g. Hunched posture, vocalises on caudal abdominal palpation, a firm 8 mm structure palpable in the caudal abdomen. Perineum stained pink, vulva closed with no discharge. Temperature 38.6°C. Teeth and cheek teeth normal on oral examination under sedation. Gut sounds present.
stages.prompt: Which findings point to the lower urinary tract?

options.label: Vocalising while passing urine
options.detail: Pain at the moment of micturition

options.label: Firm palpable structure in the caudal abdomen
options.detail: A distended, painful bladder or a calculus

options.label: Pink staining that appears at urination
options.detail: Timing ties the blood to urine, not to the vulva

options.label: Weight loss of 60 g
options.detail: A consequence of four days of pain

options.label: Reduced hay intake
options.detail: True of any painful guinea pig

stages.explanation: Guinea pigs bleed from the urinary tract and from the uterus, and the history separates them: blood that appears with a painful urination is urinary. A firm caudal abdominal structure in this species means a calculus until imaged otherwise. Anorexia and weight loss follow the pain and tell you how urgent this is, not where it is.

stages.title: Choose the tests
stages.briefing: She is stable, well hydrated, and you have one sedation to work with.

options.label: Urinalysis with sediment examination
options.detail: Crystals, blood, casts and pH

options.label: Whole-body radiographs
options.detail: Calcium-rich guinea pig stones are radio-opaque

options.label: Urine culture and sensitivity by cystocentesis
options.detail: Sterile technique, before antibiotics

options.label: Biochemistry with calcium, phosphorus, urea and creatinine
options.detail: Renal function and calcium balance

options.label: Abdominal ultrasound
options.detail: Bladder wall, ureters and the reproductive tract

options.label: Faecal parasitology
options.detail: No bearing on haematuria

options.label: Dietary vitamin C assay
options.detail: Scurvy is diagnosed on history and clinical signs, not a serum assay

stages.explanation: Sediment plus a radiograph answers most guinea pig haematuria: the stones are calcium carbonate and show up well, and the sediment tells you what is forming them. Culture matters because ascending infection and calculi travel together, and calcium with renal values shapes both the diet advice and the anaesthetic risk. A vitamin C assay is the tempting wrong turn — scurvy is a clinical diagnosis in this species.

stages.title: Interpret the results
stages.briefing: Urine: pH 8.5, 4+ blood, 2+ protein, no glucose. Sediment: sheets of calcium carbonate crystals, many red cells, no bacteria seen. Radiographs: a single 7 mm radio-opaque calculus in the bladder, no ureteral or renal opacities. Ultrasound: thickened bladder wall, uterus and ovaries normal. Calcium 2.9 mmol/L, phosphorus 1.6 mmol/L, urea 7.2 mmol/L, creatinine 62 µmol/L. Culture: no growth at 48 hours. Diet: alfalfa-based pellets ad libitum with limited grass hay.
stages.prompt: Which conclusions do the results support?

options.label: Cystic calculus with secondary cystitis
options.detail: One stone, a thick bladder wall, blood in the urine

options.label: The diet is driving stone formation
options.detail: Alfalfa ad libitum in an adult is a calcium load

options.label: Kidney function is currently preserved
options.detail: Urea and creatinine within reference

options.label: Bacterial urinary tract infection needs antibiotic cover
options.detail: Culture negative and no bacteria on sediment

options.label: Ovarian cysts are contributing to the bleeding
options.detail: Reproductive tract normal on ultrasound

stages.explanation: A negative culture in the face of an inflamed bladder is a real result, not a failed one: it means the cystitis is mechanical and antibiotics would treat nothing. The alkaline pH and carbonate crystals are expected for the species, but alfalfa ad libitum in an adult is the part you can change, and saying so is half of the treatment plan.

stages.title: Commit to a diagnosis
stages.briefing: A 7 mm radio-opaque cystic calculus, calcium carbonate crystalluria at pH 8.5, sterile urine, thickened bladder wall, normal renal values, alfalfa-based diet.

options.label: Cystic calculus with sterile secondary cystitis, diet-related
options.detail: The stone, its consequence and its cause

options.label: Bacterial cystitis
options.detail: Culture negative with no bacteria on sediment

options.label: Pyelonephritis
options.detail: No renal opacities, no azotaemia, no fever

options.label: Uterine haemorrhage from ovarian cysts
options.detail: Reproductive tract normal on ultrasound

options.label: Hypovitaminosis C
options.detail: Causes gingival and joint disease, not a radio-opaque bladder stone

stages.explanation: Naming the diet in the diagnosis is what makes the discharge advice stick: a cystotomy removes today’s stone, and moving her onto grass hay with a timothy-based pellet and free water is what stops the next one. Sterile means analgesia and surgery, not a fortnight of antibiotics.
